title: Ultimate concern
hook: Paul Tillich: faith is being grasped by what ultimately matters

segments.voice: Yesterday, Bonhoeffer's prison questions, asked from a cell in Berlin. Your line was who is Christ today? What honest answer did you jot down? Day one thousand two hundred seventy-one.

What would you give up last? Run down the list slowly: a hobby, a job, a city, money, comfort, your reputation, your plans. Somewhere near the bottom there may be something you'd keep even if all the rest went. The German theologian Paul Tillich, who later taught in America, said that thing tells you something about faith. Not because it's religious; it might not be. Because of where it sits in a life. At the bottom of the list, holding everything else up. Today, ultimate concern.

Tillich's phrase is ultimate concern. Faith, he said, is the state of being grasped by what concerns you ultimately. Notice the verb. Not grasping: grasped. You don't pick an ultimate concern the way you pick a topping. It takes hold of you, it asks for everything, and it promises, in some way, to fulfill you. Then he makes an uncomfortable point. Everyone, as Tillich saw it, has something in that place. For one person it's success, for another a nation, or a person they love. And when what sits there isn't truly ultimate, when it's something finite dressed up as everything, he called it idolatry, and said it ends in disappointment. Only God, whom he described as the ground of being, can bear that weight. Some readers connect this with the commandment Jesus called the first: "thou shalt love the Lord thy God with all thy heart, and with all thy soul, and with all thy mind, and with all thy strength." All, and all, and all. That's what an ultimate concern sounds like in scripture. And Jesus said it more plainly still: "For where your treasure is, there will your heart be also." Tillich has critics. Some say his language about God grows so abstract it loses the God who speaks and acts in the Bible. His defenders say he was trying to reach people for whom the old words had gone quiet. Either way, his question cuts close: whatever you'd give up last, can it hold what you're asking it to hold?
screen: `GRASPED, NOT GRASPING` · `FINITE THINGS DRESSED AS EVERYTHING` · `WITH ALL THY HEART` · `WHERE YOUR TREASURE IS`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: name your ultimate concern. Settle, and breathe. Ask yourself quietly: what do I give my best hours to? What would I sacrifice for? What am I most afraid of losing? Let the honest answer come, even if it surprises you, even if it isn't the one you'd say out loud. Then ask Tillich's question of it, gently: can this hold everything I'm asking it to hold? If you pray, you can offer that answer to God just as it is. The bell holds the time.
Ultimate concern. Paul Tillich's name for faith: being grasped by what matters ultimately, the thing that asks everything of you.
Your line: what matters most. Today, look at how you spend one hour, and ask what it says about what matters most to you. Day one thousand two hundred seventy-one.

howItsDone: Tillich is read in seminaries and by thoughtful seekers; some Christians use his question, what concerns me ultimately, as part of an examination of conscience or a retreat.

notes: Tillich (Dynamics of Faith) is paraphrased, not quoted; the book is under copyright. Confirm 'faith is the state of being grasped by what concerns you ultimately' is a fair paraphrase.
Tillich's link between ultimate concern and the great commandment is attributed to 'some readers'; Tillich himself discusses it, but the script keeps it soft. Confirm.
'Who later taught in America' kept general; no dates.
Idolatry and 'ends in disappointment' paraphrase Tillich's discussion of idolatrous faith; confirm.
Practice and carry stay with naming a concern; the next day (the serenity prayer) is not taught here.
Editor: 'everyone ... has something in that place' framed as Tillich's view, not a fact stated by the narrator.
Audit: smoothed a clumsy repeated name. Tillich's own wording is 'the state of being ultimately concerned'; the 'grasped' paraphrase follows the index and his discussion; confirm.
